Your Business Doesn't Have a Software Problem. It Has a Fragmented Systems Problem.
Why growing companies with plenty of software still run on spreadsheets and follow-ups, and what to do about it.
Why growing companies with plenty of software still run on spreadsheets and follow-ups, and what to do about it.

div.p: Most companies between $2M and $15M in revenue have plenty of software. A CRM for sales. An ERP or accounting system for operations. A project tool, a ticketing tool, an e-commerce platform, a few industry-specific apps.
And yet, when the CEO asks a simple question like "Can we deliver this order by Friday?", someone still has to make three phone calls and open two spreadsheets to answer it.
That isn't a software problem. Every one of those tools probably works as advertised. It's a fragmented systems problem: the tools don't share information, so people do the sharing by hand.
Nobody plans a fragmented business. It builds up one reasonable decision at a time.

Sales grows, so you buy a CRM. Operations gets complicated, so you buy an ERP or an inventory tool. Projects multiply, so someone sets up a project tracker. Each purchase solves a real bottleneck in one department.

What nobody budgets for is the space between those tools. A confirmed order in the CRM doesn't tell purchasing what to buy. Stock used on a maintenance job doesn't update the inventory count. Hours worked on a project live in a separate sheet, so profitability is a guess until month-end.

So the business fills the gaps with people. Excel becomes the unofficial glue. WhatsApp becomes the coordination layer. Your most capable employees spend their week copying data between tabs and chasing confirmations.
div.h2: The five fractures we see most often
div.p: In almost every growing company we work with, the slowdown traces back to some mix of these five:

ul.li: The data silo trap. Critical information lives in tools that don't talk to each other, so every cross-team question becomes a manual lookup.
The spreadsheet patch. Teams build unofficial trackers because they don't trust the timing of the official system.
The follow-up bottleneck. Processes move only when someone remembers to remind someone else.
The visibility lag. Dashboards exist, but leadership needs a meeting to confirm whether the numbers are right.
The disconnected stack. New tools are added on top of broken processes, which helps the business do the wrong things faster.

div.p: If two or more of these sound familiar, adding another application won't help. It will add another island.
The cost rarely shows up as a line item, which is why it survives for so long. It shows up as:

ul.li: Time. Hours every week spent re-typing orders, reconciling reports and answering "where is this?" questions.
Slower decisions. Leadership waits for last week's numbers to make today's decisions, and customers wait with them.
Errors. Every manual handoff is a chance for a wrong quantity, a missed update or a double entry.
Lost trust. When two reports disagree, people stop believing either of them, and every review meeting starts with a debate about whose numbers are correct.
Key-person risk. The business depends on the two or three people who know which spreadsheet is current.

div.h2: Why another tool won't fix it
div.p: When a team is struggling, the instinct is to buy something. A better dashboard. A new project tool. An AI assistant.

But a dashboard built on disconnected data just displays the disagreement faster. An AI assistant connected to three conflicting sources will confidently pick one of them. The new tool inherits the fragmentation underneath it.
Real improvement comes from connecting the tools that matter and retiring the ones that don't. The goal is fewer places where the same information lives, not more.
div.h2: What a connected business looks like
div.p: One of our clients, a company that manufactures products, maintains equipment and delivers projects, had grown exactly this way: a sales tracker here, a stock spreadsheet there, separate ways to log maintenance work and project hours. Month-end meant reconciling numbers that didn't match.

We moved the whole operation onto one Odoo system. Now a confirmed sales order drives what needs to be bought and made. Receipts, production and deliveries update stock as they happen. Teams log hours against real project tasks. Invoices follow completed work instead of being a separate exercise at month-end.
There was nothing dramatic about the result, and that's the point. Fewer gaps, fewer reconciliations and far fewer "which number is correct?" conversations.

blockquote.p: A connected system isn't about having more technology. It's about entering information once and letting it flow to everyone who needs it.

div.p: You don't need a company-wide transformation program to begin. Start with one question that should be easy to answer but isn't.

ol.li: Pick one everyday question. For example: "What's the real status of this customer's order?"
Trace the answer. Write down every tool, sheet, chat and person involved in answering it.
Mark the handoffs. Circle every point where someone re-types, exports, or asks someone else.
Estimate the cost. Roughly how many hours a week does that path take, and how often is the answer wrong?
Fix the most expensive handoff first. Sometimes that's an integration. Sometimes it's an ERP. Sometimes it's a single automation.

div.p: That one exercise usually tells you more about your technology needs than any vendor demo will.

If your team spends more time managing software than doing the work, the technology is failing you. Not because the tools are bad, but because nobody owns the connections between them. Fix the connections, and most of the problems people blame on software start to disappear.

The Most Dangerous Spreadsheet in Your Company Is the One You've Never Seen
Unofficial trackers are a warning sign that your systems have stopped reflecting reality. Here's how to read them.
Unofficial trackers are a warning sign that your systems have stopped reflecting reality. Here's how to read them.

div.p: When leaders think about spreadsheet risk, they usually think about the financial model. One broken formula, one wrong assumption, and the forecast is off.
That risk is real, but it's visible. Finance owns the model, people review it, and leadership knows it exists.
The more dangerous spreadsheet is the one leadership doesn't know about: the unofficial operational tracker someone created because the official system stopped reflecting reality.
They almost always start innocently, and for good reasons.

ul.li: A planner starts a private dispatch sheet because the ERP stock numbers always seem a day behind.
Sales keeps its own order tracker because customer commitments change faster than the system updates.
Production runs the floor from a WhatsApp group because the master schedule is no longer trusted.
Procurement adds another Excel layer to track what's been ordered but not yet received.

div.p: None of these people are trying to bypass your processes. They're trying to do their jobs. When the system doesn't tell them what they need, when they need it, they build something that does.
div.h2: Why it matters more than it looks
div.p: One unofficial tracker is a workaround. Five of them is a second operating system running your business, and nobody designed it.

You end up with parallel truths. Each tracker is right from its owner's point of view. Put them side by side and they disagree. Stock in the ERP says one thing, the dispatch sheet says another, and the sales tracker has already promised the customer a date based on a third.

Reporting turns political. Review meetings stop being about decisions and become arguments about whose numbers are correct. The person with the most confident spreadsheet often wins, whether or not they're right.

Your core system loses its authority. The expensive ERP or CRM you invested in becomes just one reference among many. People update it after the fact, if at all, which makes it even less reliable, which creates more side trackers.
Knowledge walks out the door. The logic inside these sheets lives in one person's head. When that person goes on leave or leaves the company, the process breaks and nobody knows why.
Shadow trackers are rarely hidden on purpose. People just don't think to mention them. A few questions usually bring them out:

ul.li: "When you need to know whether we can ship this order, where do you actually look?"
"Which report do you double-check before you trust it?"
"Is there anything you track yourself because the system doesn't show it?"
"If you were away for two weeks, what would your replacement need that isn't in the system?"

div.p: Ask these in operations, sales, planning, procurement and finance. Write down every sheet, chat group and notebook that comes up. Most leadership teams are surprised by the length of the list.
div.h2: Read the spreadsheet as a requirements document
div.p: The instinct is to ban the side trackers and force everyone back into the official system. That rarely works. The tracker exists because it meets a need the system doesn't, and banning it just drives it further underground.
A better approach is to treat each unofficial tracker as evidence. It tells you exactly what's missing.

ul.li: What does it track? That's information the system doesn't capture or doesn't show.
How often is it updated? That tells you the timing the team actually needs.
Who uses it? That tells you which handoff is broken.
What columns did they add? Those are often the fields your system is missing.

blockquote.p: Every shadow spreadsheet is a free requirements document, written by the people who know the work best.

div.h2: Fixing the cause, not the symptom
div.p: Once you know why each tracker exists, the fix is usually one of three things:

ol.li: Timing. The system has the data but updates too slowly. Real-time stock movements, automatic status changes or integrations between tools often solve this.
Visibility. The data exists but the right person can't see it in a usable way. A role-specific view or dashboard built on the live system solves this.
Missing capability. The system genuinely doesn't capture something. That's where configuration, a small custom module or a connected app comes in.

div.p: When the official system reflects reality quickly enough, people stop maintaining their own versions. Not because they were told to, but because they no longer need to.

An unofficial spreadsheet isn't a discipline problem. It's a trust problem. It tells you your team no longer believes the timing of your systems, and they're compensating by hand. Find those spreadsheets, learn from them, and fix the gap they're covering.

Why Your Leadership Team Doesn't Trust the Dashboard
A dashboard is only as reliable as the data underneath it. Here's why good-looking dashboards still start arguments.
A dashboard is only as reliable as the data underneath it. Here's why good-looking dashboards still start arguments.

div.p: Most growing companies eventually invest in an executive dashboard. The brief is always similar: one screen that shows revenue, orders, inventory, fulfillment and team output in real time.
The dashboard gets built. It looks good. And in the next review meeting, the first twenty minutes are still spent arguing about whether the numbers are right.
That isn't a design failure. It's a data failure. A dashboard is only as trustworthy as the systems feeding it.
You probably have one if any of these happen regularly:

ul.li: Someone exports the data to Excel "just to double-check" before a meeting.
Two department heads bring different numbers for the same metric.
People ask "is this up to date?" before they ask "what does this mean?"
The dashboard is opened for reviews but nobody uses it to make daily decisions.
When the dashboard and a team's own tracker disagree, the team's tracker wins.

div.p: The moment people stop believing the numbers, the dashboard becomes decoration.
div.h2: Why good dashboards show bad numbers
div.p: When the CRM, the ERP and the warehouse spreadsheet operate separately, a dashboard that pulls from all three becomes a high-speed reflection of their disagreements. Inventory says stock is available. Production says capacity is full. Sales says the customer was already promised delivery. A chart doesn't resolve that. It just gives everyone a different number to defend.

Any step where someone types, copies or uploads data is a place where errors and delays creep in. If the dashboard depends on someone updating a sheet every Monday, it's a weekly report with a nicer design.
Some sources update instantly, others nightly, others whenever someone remembers. When a dashboard mixes these, its numbers are never quite from the same moment, and they never quite add up.

"Open orders" can mean confirmed but not shipped, shipped but not invoiced, or anything not yet paid. If each team defines a metric differently, the dashboard can be technically correct and still disagree with everyone.
div.h2: Fix the foundation before the front end
div.p: Trust in data is an architecture problem, not a design problem. Before building or rebuilding a dashboard, work through these steps.

ol.li: Map where each number comes from. For every metric on the dashboard, write down the system it originates in and every step it passes through.
Give every metric one owner and one definition. Agree, in writing, what "open order", "available stock" or "gross margin" means, and who is responsible for it.
Remove manual steps. Replace uploads, exports and re-typing with direct connections between systems wherever possible.
Make systems update each other automatically. A confirmed sale should change what purchasing and production see, without anyone forwarding an email.
Show when the data was last updated. A visible timestamp tells people whether they're looking at this morning or last Thursday, and removes a lot of doubt.

blockquote.p: Clarity doesn't come from more charts. It comes from fewer places where the same number can live.

div.h2: What changes when the data is connected
div.p: When sales, purchasing, inventory, production and finance work from one connected system, the dashboard stops being a separate project. It becomes a view of data teams already enter as part of their work.
That's the real goal. Not a better-looking report, but a business where the report and reality are the same thing.
div.h2: A quick test for your next review meeting
div.p: Pick the three metrics your leadership team discusses most. For each one, ask:

ul.li: Where does this number come from?
When was it last updated?
Would every department head give the same figure if asked separately?

div.p: If you can't answer all three for every metric, the dashboard isn't the place to start. The data underneath it is.

A dashboard can look flawless and still fail to build trust. Fix the data pipeline, agree on definitions and remove manual steps, and the dashboard you already have may start working the way you hoped.

Decision Latency: The Hidden Delay Slowing Growing Companies
The biggest delays in a growing business are rarely in the work itself. They're in the decisions waiting for information.
The biggest delays in a growing business are rarely in the work itself. They're in the decisions waiting for information.

div.p: In technology, we talk a lot about latency: the delay between a request and a response. Engineers spend serious effort shaving milliseconds off it.
Inside growing companies, there's a far more expensive kind of latency, and it's measured in days. It's the delay between a question being asked and someone having the information to answer it.
We call it decision latency.
A customer asks whether you can deliver a larger order next month.

Sales needs confirmation from operations. Operations checks with planning. Planning needs to know current inventory. Inventory needs to confirm what's been ordered but not received. Finance needs to approve the credit terms.
Nothing is broken. Every person does their part. But every step depends on someone following up with someone else, and each follow-up takes hours or days.
The customer waits. Sometimes they wait somewhere else.
div.h2: Why it grows with the company
div.p: In a small company, decision latency is low because everyone sits together. The founder knows the stock, the schedule and the customer. Questions are answered across the room.
As the business grows, that changes:

ul.li: More people own pieces of the answer. No single person has the full picture anymore.
Information spreads across more tools. Each department picks its own system, and they don't share.
Approvals multiply. Controls that make sense individually stack up into long chains.
Leaders become routers. Senior people spend their day chasing updates instead of making decisions.

div.p: Hours turn into days. Days turn into weeks. Most people call this an efficiency problem. It's really an information flow problem.
Decision latency feels vague until you put a number on it. Try this with your leadership team:

ol.li: List five decisions that happen every week. For example: confirming a delivery date, approving a discount, releasing a purchase order, scheduling a job, answering a customer's status question.
Time them. For the next two weeks, note when each question is first asked and when it's answered.
Count the handoffs. How many people or systems did the answer pass through?
Find the waits. Separate the time spent actually working from the time spent waiting for someone.

div.p: Most companies find that waiting time is far larger than working time. That gap is your decision latency.
div.h3: The information isn't where the decision is made
div.p: The person deciding has to ask someone else for data that exists in a system they can't see. The fix is shared, live information: one system, or connected systems, that show each role what it needs.
When the answer is "it depends", decisions bounce between people. Writing down who decides what, and up to what limit, removes a surprising amount of delay.
div.h3: Approvals that require a person for every case
div.p: Many approvals follow simple rules: under a certain value, within standard terms, from a known supplier. Those can be automated, with only the exceptions going to a person.

blockquote.p: The fastest businesses aren't the ones with the most people or the heaviest software. They're the ones where decisions don't have to wait.

div.p: You don't need to fix every decision at once. Pick the one that waits longest and affects customers most directly, then ask:

ul.li: Can the person deciding see the information themselves?
Is it clear who is allowed to decide?
Can routine cases be approved by a rule instead of a person?
Does the system tell the next person automatically when it's their turn?

div.p: Changing even one recurring decision from "two days of follow-ups" to "answered on the spot" is often worth more than a new tool.

Decision latency hides inside normal operations. Nothing breaks, so nobody raises an alarm. But it quietly costs customers, revenue and leadership time. Measure it, find where decisions wait, and give the people deciding the information they need, when they need it.

Before You Spend on Technology, Put a Number on What the Current Way Costs
The most useful question in any technology project has nothing to do with technology.
The most useful question in any technology project has nothing to do with technology.

div.p: When a company considers a new system, an automation or an AI project, the conversation usually starts with features. What can it do? How does it compare? What does it cost?
The most useful question comes earlier, and it has nothing to do with technology:
What does the current way cost?
Without that number, a technology project gets judged on how impressive the demo looked. Six months later, nobody can say whether anything actually improved. People have opinions, but no yardstick.
With the number, everything gets easier:

ul.li: You know whether the project is worth doing at all.
You can compare options honestly.
You can set a clear target before work begins.
You can tell, afterwards, whether it worked.

div.p: You don't need a consultant or a six-week study. A rough estimate, agreed by the people who do the work, is far better than no estimate. Look at four things.
How many people touch this process, and for how long? Include the time spent gathering information, re-typing it, checking it and chasing others.
div.h3: 2. Work that has to be redone
div.p: How often does something go wrong because of a manual step? A wrong quantity, a missed update, an invoice that has to be reissued. Each one costs time to fix, and sometimes a customer's patience.
How long do customers, managers or partners wait for an answer? Waiting rarely appears in a budget, but it shows up in lost orders, slower cash collection and frustrated teams.
What could this process cost you if it fails at the wrong moment? This one is harder to estimate, but it's often the largest.
Here's a simple, illustrative calculation for a weekly sales and operations report:

ul.li: Four people spend about three hours each compiling and checking it: 12 hours a week.
About one week in four, a figure is wrong and has to be corrected: another 4 hours on average.
Decisions that depend on the report wait an average of two days for it.

div.p: That's roughly 16 hours a week, or more than 800 hours a year, before you count the cost of decisions made late or on the wrong number. Now you have something to compare a solution against.

blockquote.p: A rough number agreed by the team beats a precise number nobody believes.

div.h2: What a real baseline looked like
div.p: When we worked with Inali Foundation, a non-profit that has provided thousands of prosthetic arms across India, the starting point was clear. Patients, appointments, inventory and CSR campaigns ran on paper and spreadsheets. Finalizing a CSR campaign took seven days, and pulling a campaign report took so long that the foundation nearly lost a major recurring partner because of it.
We built one mobile and web app with role-based dashboards for each team. Afterwards, CSR campaigns were finalized in two days instead of seven.
That before-and-after made the project easy to judge. Nobody had to argue about whether it was worth it.
div.h2: Use the number to compare options honestly
div.p: Once you know what the current way costs, you can weigh four honest options:

ol.li: Build something when the process is central to how you compete and nothing off the shelf fits.
Buy a tool when the process is common and a standard product handles it well.
Fix the process when the real problem is unclear ownership, unnecessary steps or missing rules, not software.
Leave it alone when the cost turns out to be small. Sometimes the right call is to spend the money elsewhere.

div.p: That fourth option matters. A good baseline will occasionally tell you not to do the project, and that's a valuable answer too.
div.h2: A fair test for any partner
div.p: The same number is a fair test for whoever you work with, including us. Ask any vendor or partner:

ul.li: What do you think the current way is costing us?
How will we measure whether this worked?
What result would make this project not worth doing?

div.p: If a partner can't connect their proposal back to that number, keep asking questions before you sign.

Before the next technology conversation, spend an hour putting a rough number on the current way. Hours each week, work redone, decisions waiting. It will make every decision that follows clearer, and it will make success easy to recognize when it arrives.

Too Many Tools: How to Audit Your Software Stack in One Afternoon
When your team becomes the integration layer between a dozen apps, it's time to look at the whole stack, not one tool at a time.
When your team becomes the integration layer between a dozen apps, it's time to look at the whole stack, not one tool at a time.

div.p: Most businesses buy software to fix a specific bottleneck. Sales gets a CRM. Operations gets an ERP. Projects get a task tracker. Marketing gets an email platform. Support gets a helpdesk.

Each decision makes sense on its own. A few years later, a multi-million-dollar business is running on fifteen or more subscriptions, and nobody can say with confidence which system holds the actual truth.

When the tools don't talk to each other, your team becomes the integration layer. They copy data between tabs, chase approvals by email and stitch reports together by hand. That work is invisible on the software invoice, but it's often the largest cost in the stack.
div.h2: Signs your stack needs an audit

ul.li: New employees need weeks to learn which tool is used for what.
The same customer or product exists in three systems with slightly different details.
People ask "where do I find…?" more often than "how do I…?"
You're paying for features you also pay for in another tool.
Nobody is sure who owns a subscription or who still uses it.
A basic question needs data from several tools before it can be answered.

div.p: You can get most of the value from a simple exercise with a spreadsheet and the people who use the tools. Ironically, a spreadsheet is the right tool for this one.

Include everything the business pays for or depends on: core systems, small subscriptions, free tools people rely on, and shared spreadsheets that act like systems. Your finance team's card statements are a good place to start.
div.h3: Step 2: Capture five facts for each

ol.li: Owner. Who is responsible for it?
Users. How many people actually use it each week?
Cost. What do you pay per month or year, including add-ons?
Data. What information lives there that doesn't live anywhere else?
Connections. Which other tools does it exchange data with automatically, if any?

div.p: Mark every place where two tools hold the same information or do the same job. Customer records in the CRM and the accounting system. Tasks in the project tool and the helpdesk. Product data in the store and the inventory sheet.

Pick a question the business answers every day, such as "Can we deliver this order on time?" Count how many tools someone has to open to answer it. If the answer is more than one or two, you've found a priority.
div.h2: Sort every tool into four groups
div.p: With the facts in front of you, each tool falls into one of four groups:

ul.li: Keep. It does its job well, people use it, and its data is needed.
Connect. It's valuable, but it needs to exchange data automatically with the core systems so nobody re-types it.
Consolidate. Its job could be done by a system you already have. Many companies find their ERP or CRM already includes modules for things they buy separately.
Cut. Nobody uses it, or its value doesn't justify its cost and complexity.

blockquote.p: The goal isn't the fewest possible tools. It's the fewest places where the same information has to be maintained.

div.p: Subscription fees are the easy part to see. The bigger costs usually sit elsewhere:

ul.li: Manual work between tools. Hours spent moving data that should move itself.
Errors from duplicate data. Wrong addresses, prices or quantities because one copy wasn't updated.
Security and access risk. Former employees still holding logins, and customer data spread across more places than necessary.
Training and onboarding time. Every additional tool is another thing to learn.

div.p: When you add these up, consolidating or connecting a few tools often pays back much faster than the subscription savings alone suggest.
div.h2: What to do with the results
div.p: Don't try to change everything at once. Start where the audit shows the most manual work or the most important decisions:

ol.li: Connect your core flow first. Usually that's the path from lead to order to delivery to invoice.
Consolidate obvious overlaps. If your ERP already does what a separate tool does, plan a move.
Cut unused subscriptions immediately. It's quick, and it builds momentum.
Assign an owner for the stack. Someone should approve new tools and ask how they'll connect before they're bought.

div.p: Real digital infrastructure isn't about how many tools you have. It's about how smoothly information moves between them. An afternoon spent auditing your stack will show you where your team is doing the integration work by hand, and that's usually where the biggest gains are hiding.

Seven Signs You've Outgrown Spreadsheets and Need an ERP
Spreadsheets are a great way to start. Here's how to tell when they've become the thing holding your growth back.
Spreadsheets are a great way to start. Here's how to tell when they've become the thing holding your growth back.

div.p: Almost every successful company started on spreadsheets. They're flexible, cheap and everybody knows how to use them. For a small team, they're often exactly the right tool.

The trouble is that spreadsheets don't tell you when you've outgrown them. The business just gets slower, the errors get more expensive, and a few key people get busier and busier holding it all together.
Here are seven signs it's time to look seriously at an ERP.

If closing the month means matching sales, stock, purchasing and billing figures across several files before anything can go out, your data isn't connected. An ERP records each transaction once, so the numbers already agree.
div.h2: 2. Nobody fully trusts the stock numbers
div.p: When people walk to the warehouse to check, or keep their own count "just in case", your inventory records aren't keeping up with reality. In an ERP, receipts, production and deliveries update stock as they happen.
div.h2: 3. Order status requires a phone call
div.p: If answering "where is this order?" means asking three people, information is trapped in individual heads and files. In a connected system, sales can see where an order stands without asking anyone.
div.h2: 4. You learn your margins after the fact
div.p: When material costs, labor and overheads sit in separate places, true margins only appear once someone compiles them, often weeks later. An ERP can roll costs up as work happens, so you see profitability while you can still act on it.
div.h2: 5. The same data is typed more than once
div.p: An order typed into the CRM, retyped into a production sheet and typed again into an invoice is three chances to get it wrong. If re-typing is part of normal work, you're paying people to be the integration layer.
div.h2: 6. The business depends on a few people's spreadsheets
div.p: If one planner's file or one finance person's workbook is essential to daily operations, you have a key-person risk. When they're away, things slow down. When they leave, the process may leave with them.
div.h2: 7. You can't confidently answer customer questions
div.p: "Can you deliver 2,000 units by the end of the month?" should be answerable quickly. If it requires a meeting, it's costing you speed, and sometimes the order itself.

blockquote.p: If three or more of these sound familiar, your spreadsheets have probably become a bottleneck rather than a tool.

div.p: ERP stands for enterprise resource planning, which sounds more complicated than it is. In plain terms, an ERP is one system where the core parts of your business share the same data:

ul.li: Sales and customer orders
Purchasing and suppliers
Inventory and warehouses
Manufacturing or project delivery
Invoicing and accounting

div.p: Because these share one database, each step feeds the next. A confirmed order tells purchasing what to buy and production what to make. Completed work becomes an invoice. Everyone sees the same numbers.
It's worth being clear about the limits too:

ul.li: It isn't a fix for an undefined process. If nobody agrees how an order should flow, software will just make the disagreement visible.
It isn't a one-time install. The value comes from setting it up around how you work, migrating clean data and training people properly.
It isn't always a huge project. Modern platforms such as Odoo let you start with a few core apps and add more as you grow.

div.h2: When you might not need one yet
div.p: An ERP isn't always the answer. You may be better served by something smaller if:

ul.li: You have a simple operation with one main product line and few handoffs.
Your main pain is a single process, such as approvals or reporting, that an automation could fix.
Your current tools already have the features you need but aren't connected. An integration may be enough.

div.p: An honest assessment should tell you which situation you're in before anyone mentions licenses.
div.h2: How to take the next step
div.p: If you recognize several of these signs, start by mapping how one order moves through your business today: every tool, file and person it touches. That map will show you where the biggest gaps are, and it becomes the starting point for choosing and configuring any system.

Spreadsheets aren't the enemy. They're a sign of a team solving problems. But when the business depends on reconciling them, re-typing between them and trusting a few people to keep them current, they've stopped helping you grow. That's the point where one connected system starts to pay for itself.

Odoo or Custom Software? How to Choose Without Regret
An honest guide to when a standard platform fits, when custom software is worth it, and why the answer is often both.
An honest guide to when a standard platform fits, when custom software is worth it, and why the answer is often both.

div.p: "Should we use an off-the-shelf platform or build our own?" is one of the most expensive questions a growing company answers. Get it wrong one way and you force your business into software that fights you. Get it wrong the other way and you spend years paying to maintain code you didn't need.
We implement Odoo and we build custom software, and we run Hekau on Odoo ourselves. So here is the honest version of how we think about the choice.
div.h2: Start with the business, not the product
div.p: Before comparing platforms, write down how work actually moves through your company. How orders arrive, how stock is managed, how jobs are scheduled, how invoices are raised. Mark which parts are standard for your industry and which parts are genuinely different.
That distinction drives everything else.

ul.li: Standard processes like purchasing, inventory, invoicing and accounting work much the same way in most companies. A mature platform has already solved them well.

Differentiating processes are the ones that make customers choose you: a unique pricing model, a specialized service workflow, a customer experience competitors can't copy. These are where custom software can earn its cost.

div.h2: When Odoo is usually the right starting point
div.p: Odoo runs ERP, CRM, inventory, manufacturing, accounting and even your website in one system on one database. For most growing companies, that does the most for the least cost. It tends to fit well when:

ul.li: Your core processes are broadly standard for your industry.
You want sales, operations and finance on the same data quickly.
You'd rather configure proven features than pay to build and maintain them.
You want room to add modules later, such as quality, maintenance or field service, without bringing in another disconnected tool.

div.p: Odoo's Community edition has no license fee, and because it's open source, you aren't locked into a single vendor. Some apps are only in the Enterprise edition, so it's worth knowing exactly what your edition includes before you commit.
div.h2: When custom software is worth it
div.p: Custom development makes sense when:

ul.li: The process is your competitive edge. If the way you do something is why customers buy from you, bending it to fit a standard product can cost you that edge.
You need a customer- or vendor-facing platform. Portals, marketplaces and specialized apps often need a tailored experience.
The standard product genuinely can't do it. After a careful fit-gap analysis, some requirements simply have no good standard answer.
You're building a product, not running a process. Software you sell or that defines your service usually needs to be your own.

div.h2: The most common answer: a mix
div.p: In practice, many of the best setups combine both. Odoo runs the standard back office: sales, purchasing, stock, accounting. Custom software handles what's unique: a customer portal, a specialized field app or an integration with a machine or third-party platform. Integrations keep the two in sync so data is entered once.

blockquote.p: Use standard software for what's standard and custom software for what makes you different. Then connect them.

div.h2: Run a fit-gap analysis before you decide
div.p: A fit-gap analysis compares your processes to what a platform does out of the box. For each step in your process, mark one of three outcomes:

ol.li: Fit. The standard feature does what you need.
Configurable. The platform can do it with settings, workflows or reports.
Gap. It genuinely needs custom work or a different tool.

div.p: If most of your process falls into the first two groups, a standard platform is likely the right foundation. If the gaps cluster in the processes that make you different, that's where custom work belongs.
div.h2: Think about cost over five years, not one
div.p: The first-year price is misleading. Compare total cost over several years:

ul.li: Licenses and hosting. Recurring platform and infrastructure costs.
Implementation or build. The upfront project.
Customization and maintenance. Every piece of custom code has to be maintained, tested and upgraded.
Upgrades. Heavily customized platforms become expensive to upgrade. Using standard features before custom code keeps upgrades cheap.
People. Training, support and the internal time needed to run it.

div.p: A platform that seems cheaper on day one can become expensive if it's customized heavily. A custom build that seems expensive can be good value if it replaces several tools and becomes a lasting advantage.
div.h2: Questions to ask any implementation partner

ul.li: Which parts of our process would you keep standard, and which would you customize?
What happens to our customizations when the platform releases a new version?
What does our edition include, and what would need an upgrade?
Who owns the code and the data?
If you think we don't need custom work, will you tell us?

div.p: The choice isn't really "Odoo or custom". It's "what's standard about our business, and what's different?" Put the standard parts on a proven platform, invest custom effort only where it creates an advantage, and make sure everything is connected. That's the approach least likely to leave you with regrets.

What a Good ERP Rollout Looks Like (and Why So Many Go Wrong)
Most ERP problems aren't caused by the software. They come from how the rollout is planned and run.
Most ERP problems aren't caused by the software. They come from how the rollout is planned and run.

div.p: An ERP should make a business calmer: fewer reconciliations, fewer "which number is correct?" conversations, and decisions based on today's data. Yet many companies remember their ERP project as the most stressful year they've had.
In most cases, the software wasn't the problem. The rollout was.
The same patterns show up again and again:

ul.li: Everything goes live at once. Every team switches on the same day, problems multiply, and nobody has time to fix them properly.
The software is customized to copy old habits. Instead of improving the process, the project recreates the spreadsheets inside the new system, at great cost.
Data migration is left until the end. Old, inconsistent data is loaded in a hurry, and day one starts with wrong numbers.
Training happens once. A single session before go-live, then people are left to work it out.
The partner disappears at go-live. Just when real use exposes the gaps, support ends.
Leadership delegates and steps away. Without decisions from the top, the project stalls on every disagreement.

div.p: A well-run rollout follows a clear sequence. Here's the approach we use.

Walk through how orders, stock, customers, production and billing move today, and where they break. Talk to the people who do the work, not just the managers. This is where you find the unofficial spreadsheets and workarounds that the new system needs to replace.

Match your processes to the platform's standard features. List the real gaps. Agree on phases, costs and how you'll measure success. A good rule: use standard features before custom code wherever the standard approach is good enough. It keeps the project faster and future upgrades cheaper.
Set up the apps, build custom pieces only where they're needed, and integrate the tools you're keeping. Show working software to the teams early and often, so they can steer before it's finished.

Move customers, products, open orders and balances across, then check them against the old system so day one starts with real numbers. Train each team on its own daily tasks, using its own data, not a generic demo.
Go live in phases where possible, so each team is productive before the next one moves. Then stay close through the first month-end close and beyond, fixing and improving as people use it for real.

blockquote.p: A rollout isn't finished when the system goes live. It's finished when the first month-end closes cleanly and teams stop keeping their old spreadsheets.

div.p: Moving one area at a time, such as sales and inventory first, then manufacturing, then accounting, has clear advantages:

ul.li: Problems are smaller and easier to fix.
Each team gets proper attention during its switch.
Early wins build confidence for the next phase.
Each phase is useful before the next one starts.

div.p: Data migration is often treated as a technical afterthought. It shouldn't be. If the customer list has duplicates, the product codes are inconsistent and opening stock is wrong, the new system will be distrusted from the first day.
Start cleaning data early. Decide what history you actually need to bring across. Run test migrations and have the people who know the data check the results.
An ERP project changes how the whole company works, so it can't be fully delegated. Leaders make the difference by:

ol.li: Naming one accountable owner inside the business, with the authority to make decisions.
Freeing up key people's time. The experts on your processes are also your busiest people. Plan for the hours they'll need.
Settling disagreements quickly. When two departments want the process to work differently, someone has to decide.
Using the system themselves. When leaders ask for numbers from the new system rather than from old spreadsheets, everyone else follows.

div.p: In the first three months after go-live, look for:

ul.li: Month-end closing faster than before.
Fewer manual reconciliations between departments.
Unofficial spreadsheets being abandoned.
People answering customer questions without asking another team.
Reports coming from the system rather than being compiled by hand.

div.p: ERP success depends far more on how the rollout is run than on which platform you choose. Map the real process, keep customization to what's necessary, migrate clean data, train properly, go live in phases and choose a partner who stays after launch. Do those things, and the ERP becomes the calm, connected foundation it was meant to be.

Ending Manual Production Reporting: Connecting the Shop Floor to Your ERP
For many manufacturers, the ERP knows what was planned and the shop floor knows what happened. The gap between them is where time and margin disappear.
For many manufacturers, the ERP knows what was planned and the shop floor knows what happened. The gap between them is where time and margin disappear.

div.p: A production head once described a problem to us that we hear in some form at almost every manufacturer: "We have all the data. We just don't have time to trust it."

On paper, everything is in place. The ERP is running. The machines generate data. Reports are available. But to answer a simple question like "Can we fulfill this order on time?", people still call the inventory team, check with production, ask procurement and reconfirm with planning.

The reason is usually the same. The ERP knows what was planned. The shop floor knows what actually happened. And the two only meet when someone types the shop floor's numbers into the system, often at the end of a shift, sometimes at the end of the week.
div.h2: What manual production reporting looks like

ul.li: Operators write output, scrap and downtime on paper or whiteboards.
Supervisors compile shift reports in spreadsheets.
Quality test results are recorded by hand, then entered later.
Production updates are shared on WhatsApp groups.
Someone in planning re-types it all into the ERP.

div.p: Every step adds delay and every re-typed number is a chance for error. By the time the data reaches management, it describes yesterday, and nobody is fully sure it's right.

ul.li: Late decisions. Problems on the line are discovered after the shift, not during it.
Unreliable delivery promises. Sales can't see real progress, so commitments are based on hope or phone calls.
Hidden losses. Downtime, scrap and slow cycles are under-reported when they're logged by hand.
Inaccurate costs and margins. If actual material use and labor aren't captured, product costs are estimates.
Quality risk. A transcription error in a test record is a quality problem waiting to surface.
Supervisor time. Skilled people spend hours compiling reports instead of improving production.

div.h2: What a connected shop floor looks like
div.p: The principle is simple: capture data once, at the source, and let it flow to the ERP automatically.
div.h3: Capture at the machine or workstation
div.p: Where machines can share data, connect them directly. Where they can't, give operators a simple tablet or phone screen at the workstation to record output, scrap and downtime as it happens, with large buttons and minimal typing.
div.h3: Use an MES or machine monitoring layer where it fits
div.p: A manufacturing execution system (MES) or machine monitoring platform tracks what's happening on the floor in real time: which jobs are running, at what speed and with what stoppages. On its own, it's another silo. Connected to the ERP, it becomes the bridge between plan and reality.

Whether you run Odoo, Epicor or another ERP, the aim is the same. Work orders flow down to the floor, and actual production, material consumption and quality results flow back up, without anyone re-typing them.
div.h3: Show it to the people who decide
div.p: Dashboards built on live data let planners, sales and leadership see progress and problems as they happen, instead of waiting for a compiled report.

blockquote.p: The number in the system should be the number the machine produced, not the number someone remembered to type in later.

div.p: One of our clients, an industrial manufacturer whose products are tested against strict quality standards, recorded test results by hand. It was slow, error-prone and hard to analyze, and every error in a test record was a quality risk.

We built an Android app that connects directly to the testing machines and records results in real time. Results travel over encrypted connections to a central server and appear on a web platform where authorized users see only the data sets relevant to them. Charts and custom dashboards make trends and anomalies easy to spot.
The outcome: no manual entry errors, results available the moment a test finishes, and managers who see trends without compiling anything.
Connecting an entire factory at once is rarely the right first move. Start small and prove the value:

ol.li: Pick one line, cell or test station where manual reporting causes the most delay or error.
Decide which three or four data points matter most, such as good output, scrap, downtime reasons and test results.
Capture them at the source, by machine connection or a simple operator screen.
Connect that data to your ERP so work orders, stock and costs update automatically.
Measure the difference in reporting time, data accuracy and how quickly problems are spotted.
Expand line by line once the approach is working and trusted.

ul.li: How long after a shift ends does management see its real output?
How many times is a production number written or typed before it reaches the ERP?
How confident is sales in the delivery dates it gives customers?
Do you know your actual scrap and downtime, or an estimate?

div.p: Most manufacturers don't lack data. They lack connected data that arrives in time to act on. Closing the gap between the shop floor and the ERP turns production reporting from an end-of-shift chore into live visibility, and turns "let me check and get back to you" into an answer on the spot.

Workflow Automation: Where to Start When Everything Feels Manual
You don't need to automate everything. You need to automate the right thing first.
You don't need to automate everything. You need to automate the right thing first.

div.p: Ask any growing team what slows them down and you'll hear a familiar list. Re-typing data. Chasing approvals. Sending the same reminders. Compiling the same weekly report. Copying information from one tool to another.
Each task is small on its own. Together, they can consume a large share of your team's week, and they're often done by the people you most need focused on customers.
That's the case for automation. The harder question is where to start.
If someone re-types the same data every day, it's a candidate for automation.
More broadly, look for work that is:

ul.li: Repetitive. It happens often, in roughly the same way each time.
Rule-based. A clear rule decides what should happen, with few judgment calls.
Between systems. Data moves from one tool to another by hand.
Time-sensitive. Delays cause problems for customers or other teams.

div.p: Most companies have opportunities in these areas:

ul.li: Data entry and transfer. Orders, leads, customer details or timesheets moved between systems by hand.
Approvals. Purchase requests, discounts and expenses that follow clear rules but wait for a person every time.
Follow-ups and reminders. Appointment reminders, payment reminders, quote follow-ups and task nudges.
Reports. Weekly or daily reports compiled by copying figures from several sources.
Documents. Contracts, confirmations and receipts generated from details already in the system.
Notifications. Telling the next person or the customer when something changes.

div.h2: How to rank what to automate first
div.p: Don't start with the most interesting automation. Start with the one that pays for itself fastest. For each candidate, estimate:

ol.li: Frequency. How often does it happen each week?
Time. How long does it take each time, including chasing and checking?
Error cost. What happens when it goes wrong?
Stability. Is the process settled, or does it change every month?

div.p: High frequency, meaningful time, costly errors and a stable process: that's your first automation. Start with the costliest step, prove the value, then expand.

blockquote.p: Small, measurable wins first. Bigger workflows once the team trusts the automations.

div.h2: What it looks like in practice
div.p: An event ticketing marketplace we built needed to onboard event organizers without a team drafting paperwork. Now, as soon as an organizer completes registration, the platform builds their contract from the details they entered and emails it to both sides. The marketplace serves 6,000 regular users and a growing vendor base, with no manual contract drafting.

MyWanderloop depends on verification codes and alerts arriving on time. We integrated automated SMS and email through MSG91, using compliant templates and webhooks, so every message is sent automatically and tracked from send to delivery.
div.h3: Reminders that cut calls and no-shows
div.p: For Inali Foundation, appointment booking now triggers automatic reminders and updates for patients and staff, which cuts no-shows and phone calls. It's one part of the app that cut CSR campaign turnaround from seven days to two.
Automation amplifies whatever process it runs on. Be careful with:

ul.li: Unsettled processes. If the steps change every few weeks, fix the process first.
Rare exceptions. Automating a case that happens twice a year rarely pays back.
Judgment-heavy decisions. Automate the information gathering, and leave the judgment to a person.
Broken processes. Automating a bad process just helps you do the wrong thing faster.

div.h2: Five steps to automation that sticks

ol.li: Analyze the process. Trace each workflow and note where data is re-typed, chased or lost.
Plan and prioritize. Rank candidates by hours saved and risk, and agree which come first.
Design the workflow. Write down triggers, rules, approvals and notifications before anything is built.
Build and connect. Build the automation into the systems your team already uses, and test it against real cases.
Monitor and improve. Watch it in daily use, handle edge cases and extend what works.

div.p: Every automation needs an owner: a person who knows what it does, notices when it fails and decides when it should change. Without an owner, automations quietly break and people go back to doing the work by hand.

You don't need a grand automation strategy to get started. Find the manual step that happens most often and costs the most time, automate it properly, and measure the hours you get back. That first win usually funds, and justifies, the next one.

No Company Is AI-Ready. Some Workflows Are.
"Getting the company AI-ready" sounds sensible and tends to stall. Judging one workflow at a time works better.
"Getting the company AI-ready" sounds sensible and tends to stall. Judging one workflow at a time works better.

div.p: Many leadership teams have set a goal along the lines of "get our data AI-ready". It sounds responsible. Before investing in AI, make sure the foundation is in place.

The trouble is that it's a company-wide project with no clear finish line. Company-wide projects tend to stall before anything useful ships. Months later, the data is a bit cleaner, nobody is using AI for anything that matters, and the budget is gone.
A more useful way to look at it: no company is AI-ready, but some workflows are.
div.h2: Three tests for a ready workflow
div.p: A single workflow is much easier to judge than a whole company. We'd call a workflow ready for AI when three things are true.
div.h3: 1. It happens often, and roughly the same way each time
div.p: Repetition is where AI earns its keep. A task that happens hundreds of times a month, following a similar pattern, gives AI something to learn from and plenty of chances to save time. A task that happens twice a quarter, differently each time, rarely justifies the effort.
div.h3: 2. Its inputs come from one place
div.p: If someone has to gather the inputs from three tools before the work can start, that gathering is the real problem to fix first. AI that has to work across scattered, inconsistent sources will produce scattered, inconsistent results.
div.h3: 3. Someone can tell a right answer from a wrong one
div.p: If nobody can check the output quickly, nobody will trust it for long. The best early AI workflows have outputs a person can verify at a glance.

blockquote.p: Look for the workflow that already passes all three tests. That's a better first AI project than the ambitious one.

div.p: Workflows that often pass all three tests include:

ul.li: Order status updates. Frequent, rule-based and easy to check against the system.
Quote follow-ups. A predictable pattern with clear inputs from the CRM.
Invoice matching. Comparing invoices with purchase orders and receipts.
Ticket triage. Sorting and routing support requests to the right team.
Document checks. Reviewing documents against a defined standard or checklist.

div.p: None of these are glamorous. That's exactly why they work. They're common, measurable and low-risk, and they build the confidence needed for bigger projects.
div.h2: Why the ambitious project usually fails first
div.p: The first AI idea in many companies is a big one: predict demand across the whole business, or build an assistant that can answer any question about the company. These ideas fail all three tests at once. They depend on data from many sources, they cover many different situations, and it's hard to know whether the answer is right.
Start where success is easy to recognize. The bigger cleanup can follow once something is working.
Try this with your leadership team. List ten workflows that take up meaningful time. For each one, answer yes or no:

ol.li: Does it happen at least weekly, in a similar way each time?
Do its inputs come from one system?
Can a person check the output quickly?

div.p: The workflows with three yeses are your candidates. The ones with two yeses tell you what to fix, often an integration so the inputs come from one place. The ones with fewer are not where to begin.
div.h2: Readiness often has nothing to do with AI
div.p: One of the best examples of AI readiness in our own work had no AI in it at all. MaxintelB2B came to us because its website wasn't turning visitors into leads. We rebuilt the navigation, created focused landing pages and connected lead capture to HubSpot. Conversions rose 15% and high-intent leads rose 30%.

If MaxintelB2B wants AI to score or route its leads in future, it will depend on what that project put in place: every lead landing in one system, with consistent information. The foundation came first, and it delivered results on its own.

Stop asking whether your company is AI-ready. Ask which of your workflows are. Pick one that happens often, draws from one source and has outputs someone can check. Make that work, measure it, and let the next project build on it.

Most AI Plans Start at Step Three. Start at Step Two Instead.
The difference between adding AI and embedding it comes down to the step most teams skip.
The difference between adding AI and embedding it comes down to the step most teams skip.

div.p: Most AI plans start at step three.
Step three is the tool: which model, which vendor, how many licenses. It's the most visible decision, so it's usually where the conversation starts. Vendors are happy to start there too.
But there are two steps that should come first, and the second one is where most AI projects are won or lost.
div.h2: Step one: choose the work you want to change
div.p: Most teams get here, even if loosely. "We want AI to help with customer service." "We want to speed up quoting." "We want better forecasts."
The more specific, the better. "Reduce the time to answer order status questions" is more useful than "improve customer service with AI".
div.h2: Step two: redraw the work with AI inside it
div.p: This is the step that gets skipped. Before choosing any tool, sketch how the work will actually run once AI is part of it. Answer four questions:

ol.li: Which step goes away? What does a person no longer have to do?
Which step changes? What does a person now do differently?
What does a person check before acting on the output? Where does human judgment stay?
What happens when the output is wrong? How is it caught, corrected and learned from?

div.p: When step two is done, step three gets smaller. The tool choice often becomes obvious. And sometimes it turns out a cleaner handoff or a simple integration does the job, and you don't need AI for it at all.

blockquote.p: If you can't draw the workflow on one page with the AI step in it, you aren't ready to pick a tool.

div.h2: What happens when step two is skipped
div.p: The tool gets placed on top of the old process. And the old process usually wins.
That's how many AI pilots end. Not with a dramatic failure, but with a slow fade. The demo worked. Then nobody opened it again.
The causes are usually structural, and the model is rarely the issue:

ul.li: It can't reach live data. It runs on an export or a copy, so the answers are always a little behind, and people stop trusting them.
Nobody owns the outcome. The pilot belongs to a team, but no one is accountable for whether it changes a result.
It sits outside the workflow. To use it, someone has to leave their tool, open another one and carry the answer back. That extra step is the first thing to go when the week gets busy.

div.p: Adding AI means giving people a new tool and hoping they use it. The work looks the same, with an optional extra step.

Embedding AI means the workflow itself has changed. The AI step is part of how the work runs. Its output lands where the next person already works, so it gets acted on instead of copied somewhere else.
The difference is almost entirely decided in step two.
div.h2: Three things to settle before any pilot
div.p: Before starting an AI pilot, agree on three things:

ol.li: Which live system it reads from. Not an export, not a copy.
Who owns the result. A named person accountable for whether it changes an outcome.
Where its output lands. Inside the tool the next person already uses.

div.p: If those three are unanswered, the pilot is a demo with a longer runtime.
div.h2: A simple exercise for your next meeting
div.p: Take the AI idea your team is most excited about. On one page, draw:

ul.li: The workflow today, step by step.
The same workflow with the AI step in it.
Where a person reviews the output.
What happens when it's wrong.
Where the result goes next.

div.p: If the drawing is easy, you're ready to talk about tools. If it's hard, you've just saved yourself an expensive pilot.

The tool is the last decision, not the first. Choose the work, redraw it with AI inside, and settle the data, ownership and handoff before any demo. That's the difference between AI that's added and AI that's embedded.

Licenses and weekly users measure access. Here's how to tell whether the work itself has changed.

div.p: Many companies now give their employees access to AI tools. Licenses are bought, training sessions are held and usage numbers go up.
Then someone in the leadership team asks a fair question: what has actually changed?

Often the honest answer is: not much. People write emails faster and summarize documents more easily. That's useful. But the way the business works, how orders flow, how decisions get made, how customers are served, looks the same as before.
That's the difference between access and adoption.
Here's a quick test for whether your company uses AI or only has access to it.
Ask five people on your team to name one task or decision that works differently now because of AI.
"Differently" means something specific:

ul.li: A step that no longer exists.
A handoff that no longer waits.
A decision made from information that used to take a day to pull together.

div.p: If the answers sound like "I use it to draft emails" or "I ask it questions", that's access. It's useful, but it's personal. The work itself looks the same.
Adoption has three features:

ol.li: A workflow has an AI step in it. It's part of how the work runs, not an optional extra.
Someone owns that step. A named person is accountable for whether it works.
The output lands where the next person already works. It gets acted on, instead of being copied into another tool.

blockquote.p: Licenses, seats and weekly users measure access. None of them tell you whether the work changed.

div.h2: The question nobody asks: who acts on the answer?
div.p: There's a second reason AI often fails to change outcomes, and it has nothing to do with the technology.
Imagine an AI tool flags a late shipment on Tuesday. The order still ships late on Friday. The alert was right.
The problem was that everyone who saw it was waiting for someone else to decide:

ul.li: Sales could see it, but had no say over the production schedule.
Planning could reschedule, but needed approval to expedite.
Purchasing could expedite, but hadn't been told the customer was at risk.

div.p: The AI did its part. The company had never decided who acts on an answer like that.
A lot of AI effort goes into training people to ask better questions. Far less goes into deciding who is allowed to act on the answers.
For every AI output your team relies on, ask two questions:

li.strong: Who is expected to act on it?

div.p: If the answer is "it depends", that's where the value is stuck. The fix isn't more AI. It's clearer ownership: who decides, up to what limit, and who needs to be told.
div.h2: Better questions for the next AI budget conversation
div.p: Instead of asking how many people are using AI, ask:

ul.li: Which workflows have changed because of AI in the last six months?
Which steps no longer exist?
How much time or money has each change saved?
For each AI output, who acts on it, and do they have the authority to?

div.p: If the list of changed workflows is short, that's not a failure. It's a clear starting point. Pick one workflow, embed AI properly and measure the result before expanding.
The best first step is usually small and specific:

ul.li: Choose one recurring workflow that already passes basic readiness tests: frequent, inputs from one place, easy to check.
Redesign it with the AI step inside it.
Name an owner and confirm they can act on the output.
Put the output where the next person already works.
Measure what changed after a month.

div.p: Access is easy to buy. Adoption has to be designed. Ask your team what works differently because of AI, and make sure someone is allowed to act on what it tells you. That's how AI moves from a personal productivity tool to a real change in how your business runs.

Bad Data Is More Expensive Once AI Is Involved
People quietly work around unreliable numbers. AI doesn't know it should, and it answers with confidence anyway.
People quietly work around unreliable numbers. AI doesn't know it should, and it answers with confidence anyway.

div.p: Every team has a number it quietly ignores.
The sales report that runs a week behind. The stock sheet nobody updates on weekends. The customer list with three spellings of the same company.
People cope. They know which figure to trust and which to double-check. Nobody wrote that down. It lives in people's heads.
That arrangement works, more or less, as long as people are the ones reading the data. It stops working the moment you connect an AI assistant to the same sources.
div.h2: Why AI makes bad data more expensive
div.p: Connect an AI assistant to your systems and ask a plain question: how many orders are open?
It will answer in one clear, confident sentence.

It has no idea the sales report runs a week behind. It doesn't know the stock sheet skips weekends, or that "ABC Industries", "ABC Ind." and "A.B.C. Industries" are the same customer. It picks a number and sounds sure about it.
A person hesitates when a number looks off. A fluent answer doesn't invite the same doubt, so the wrong figure travels further: into a customer email, a planning decision or a board update.

blockquote.p: AI doesn't create bad data. It removes the hesitation that used to protect you from it.

div.p: Before AI reads your systems, read them yourself. An AI tool works with whatever it finds and treats all of it as reliable, including:

ul.li: Reports someone stitches together by hand. They depend on one person's process and timing.
Decisions agreed in chats. The discount approved on WhatsApp never reached the system.
Data typed into two places. The CRM and the ERP each have a version, and they've drifted apart.
Fields used inconsistently. One team uses a field for delivery dates, another for promised dates.
Stale records. Old customers, discontinued products and closed projects still marked as active.

div.p: Here's the useful part. Your team already knows most of these problems. They've built workarounds for them.
Before connecting AI to anything, write down the workarounds your team already uses:

ol.li: Which report is late? And by how much?
Which sheet is wrong? And what do people check instead?
Which field gets typed three different ways? Customer names, product codes, units.
Which numbers need a phone call to confirm? Those are the ones the system doesn't reflect.
Which decisions live outside the system? Approvals in email or chat that never get recorded.

div.p: That list is your data cleanup plan, and it already exists. You just haven't written it down.
div.h2: Fix the sources, not just the data
div.p: Cleaning data once helps for a while. Fixing why it gets messy helps for good. For each problem on your list, ask what causes it:

ul.li: A late report usually means a manual step or a slow integration. Automate it.
Duplicate records usually mean data entered in two systems. Connect them, or pick one as the master.
Inconsistent fields usually mean unclear definitions. Agree on them and enforce them with dropdowns and validation.
Decisions in chats usually mean the system makes recording them too hard. Make the official path the easy path.

div.h2: Start with the data your first AI use case needs
div.p: You don't need to clean everything before using AI. Focus on the data behind the one workflow you want to improve first. If the use case is order status, make sure order, shipment and stock data are reliable and current. Leave the rest for later.
That keeps the work small, makes the benefit visible quickly, and builds trust in the AI from its first answer.

Your people protect you from bad data every day by knowing what not to trust. AI can't do that. Before connecting it to your systems, write down the numbers everyone quietly ignores, fix the reasons they're unreliable, and start with the data your first use case depends on.

Private AI: Why Public Tools Don't Know Your Margins
Public AI tools are good at drafting and summarizing. Real operational value comes from AI that works on your own data, inside your control.
Public AI tools are good at drafting and summarizing. Real operational value comes from AI that works on your own data, inside your control.

div.p: Using a public AI chatbot doesn't make a business AI-enabled.

Public AI tools are powerful. They help people draft, summarize and analyze. But they don't understand your margins. They can't see your live inventory. They don't know your production constraints, your customer terms or your supplier history.
Without your internal data, AI is a smart assistant. With it, connected properly and kept under your control, it can become a real operational tool.
div.h2: What public tools can and can't do

ul.li: Drafting emails, proposals and documents.
Summarizing long text and meeting notes.
Answering general questions and explaining concepts.
Helping individuals work faster.

p.strong: What they can't do on their own:

ul.li: Tell you whether a new order will hurt your margin.
Spot that a supplier is consistently late on a critical part.
Flag that a production bottleneck will delay next week's deliveries.
Answer questions about your business using today's numbers.

div.p: The difference is data. Operational value depends on your own records, and they don't live in a public tool.
div.h2: The data question every leader should ask
div.p: As AI use spreads, one question keeps coming up in leadership conversations: what about our data?

It's the right question. When employees paste information into public tools, it can include customer data, pricing logic, contract terms and internal financials. Even when a tool's policies are sound, many companies don't have a clear view of what's being shared, by whom and where it goes.
That's a governance problem, and it grows quietly as more people use more tools.
Private, or in-house, AI means building AI capabilities on top of your own systems, in environments you control. In practice:

ul.li: Your data stays in your environment. Customer records, pricing and vendor contracts aren't sent to tools you don't control.
Access follows roles. People see AI outputs based on the same permissions they have in your systems.
Everything is logged. You can see what data was used, by whom and what came out.
It's connected to the tools people already use. Outputs appear in your ERP, CRM or apps, not in a separate window.

blockquote.p: Data privacy isn't a feature you add to AI later. It's the foundation you build it on.

div.h2: What it can do for operations
div.p: When AI sits on top of clean, connected ERP and CRM data, it can do things public tools can't:

ul.li: Flag margin risks before an order is confirmed, by comparing pricing, costs and terms against history.
Spot procurement issues early, such as suppliers whose delivery times are slipping.
Surface bottlenecks automatically, in production, approvals or fulfillment.
Answer operational questions using current data, with links back to the records behind the answer.
Score and route work, such as leads, tickets or documents, using your own patterns.

div.h2: Models trained on your own patterns
div.p: Some of the most useful AI is narrow and specific to one business. Two examples from our work:

ul.li: For Mohur, a platform connecting investors with startups, we built a machine-learning engine that recommends startups to investors and investors to startups, and keeps learning as the platform grows.
For a job posting platform, we built a scoring system that rates every job post on quality, relevance and completeness, feeding the platform's own AI model and its employers' dashboards.

div.p: Neither depends on a general-purpose chatbot. Both work because they're built on the platform's own data and goals.
div.h2: What has to be in place first
div.p: Private AI is only as good as the foundation underneath it. Before investing, check:

ol.li: Clean, connected core data. ERP, CRM, production and inventory records that agree with each other.
Clear access rules. Who should see what, already defined in your systems.
A specific first use case. One decision or workflow where better information would save time or money.
An owner. Someone accountable for whether the AI changes a result.
A way to check outputs. People who can tell a good answer from a bad one, especially early on.

div.h2: Questions to ask any AI vendor or partner

ul.li: Where will our data be stored and processed?
Will our data be used to train models for anyone else?
How are access permissions enforced?
Can we see logs of what data the AI used and what it produced?
What happens to our data if we stop working with you?
Who owns the models and code built for us?

div.p: If the answers are vague, keep asking before any data moves.

Public AI tools are useful for individuals. Operational value comes from AI that works on your own data: your margins, your inventory, your constraints. Build it on a connected foundation, keep it inside your control, and start with one decision where better information clearly pays off.

A Demo Is Not a Product: What We Learned Building an AI Assistant for a Newsroom
A behind-the-scenes look at how an AI assistant for The Arc took several rounds of building to fit real editorial work.
A behind-the-scenes look at how an AI assistant for The Arc took several rounds of building to fit real editorial work.

div.p: It took us several builds to get the AI assistant for The Arc right.

The brief sounded simple. The Arc is a news platform covering India's high-growth companies, and its editors check every article against a detailed house style. We set out to build an assistant that could help with that checking.

We started early in 2025. Checks and safeguards were in place from the first version. But the prompts and guidance were still some way from the output we actually wanted. So we kept building, and every version taught us something.
div.h2: Lesson 1: A demo can look finished very quickly
div.p: Modern AI makes impressive demos easy. Within days, you can show an assistant reading an article and producing suggestions. It looks done.

It isn't. A demo shows that something is possible. A product has to work on real articles, by real writers, under real deadlines, consistently enough that editors rely on it. The gap between those two is where most of the work lives.

blockquote.p: A demo answers "can it do this?" A product answers "can we rely on it every day?"

div.h2: Lesson 2: The output format matters as much as the answer
div.p: The way the assistant reported its findings changed three times.

ol.li: First, a format built for machines. Structured and precise, but hard for an editor to read quickly.
Then, plain language. Easier to read, but editors still had to work out why each suggestion mattered.
Then, a form where each suggestion pointed to the rule behind it. Editors could see the issue, the suggested fix and the house-style rule in one place, and decide quickly.

div.p: Each change came from understanding the work a little better. The AI's underlying ability didn't change much between versions. What changed was how well its output fit the way editors actually work.
div.h2: Lesson 3: Write the standard down properly
div.p: An assistant can only check against a standard that's clearly defined. Much of a house style lives in experienced editors' heads: preferences, exceptions, judgment calls. Turning that into guidance an AI can follow forced useful clarity about what the rules actually were.

This applies far beyond publishing. If your team checks work against a standard, such as quality checks, compliance reviews or document approvals, the first step is making sure the standard is written down clearly enough for someone new to follow.
div.h2: Lesson 4: Safeguards come first, not last
div.p: Checks and safeguards were part of the very first build, not something added before launch. The assistant suggests and the editor decides. That kept the risk low while we refined everything else, and it meant editors could trust it enough to keep using it while it improved.
div.h2: Lesson 5: Budget for rounds, not a single build
div.p: The part of AI projects people underestimate is the iteration: several rounds of building, testing with real users and refining. That isn't a sign of a project going wrong. It's how a tool comes to fit real work.
When planning an AI project, budget time and money for those rounds from the start. A plan that assumes one build and a launch is planning for a demo.

The assistant is in usable form and helps The Arc's editors check articles against their house style. It came out of a long technology partnership. We originally took over The Arc's platform after its previous vendor walked away mid-build, and it now serves 50,000+ visitors a month.
div.h2: What this means for your AI plans
div.p: If you're considering an AI tool for your own team, a few questions are worth asking early:

ul.li: Is the standard the AI will work to written down clearly?
Who will test it on real work, and how often?
How should the output look so the person using it can act quickly?
Where does a person stay in control?
Have we planned for several rounds of refinement, not one?

div.p: AI projects that fit real work take longer than the demo suggests, and that's normal. Define the standard, keep a person in control, shape the output around how people work, and plan for several rounds. The result is a tool people rely on, not one they try once and forget.
