Your Vendor Walked Away Mid-Build. Here's How to Rescue the Project.
A practical recovery plan for leaders left with half-finished software, a slipping launch date and code nobody understands.
A practical recovery plan for leaders left with half-finished software, a slipping launch date and code nobody understands.

div.p: It's one of the most stressful situations a business leader can face with technology. The development vendor has stopped responding, or quit, or delivered something that doesn't work. The launch date keeps slipping. The team depends on a platform that's only half built, and nobody fully understands the code.
The good news: most stalled projects can be recovered. The key is to make the first decisions calmly and in the right order.
Before anything else, make sure you have control of your assets. Get access to, or confirm you already own:

ul.li: The source code repository, with full history.
Hosting and cloud accounts, including billing.
Third-party services, such as payment gateways, email, SMS and analytics.
App store accounts, if you have mobile apps.
Credentials and API keys used by the system.
Any documentation, designs and requirement documents.

div.p: If these are in the vendor's name, move them into your company's name as soon as possible. Then change passwords and keys that the previous vendor had access to.
div.h2: Step 2: Audit before you promise a date
div.p: The temptation is to bring in a new team and ask, "When can you finish it?" Any honest team will say they can't answer until they've seen what exists.
A proper code and project audit reviews:

ul.li: Code quality. Is it readable, consistent and maintainable?
Architecture. Is the structure sound enough to build on?
Security. Are there vulnerabilities that need urgent fixing?
Performance. Will it hold up under real traffic and data?
Missing features. What was promised but not built?
Deployment setup. Can it be released reliably?
Documentation. Can someone new understand it?

div.p: The audit should end with a clear view of what you actually have, not a sales pitch.
div.h2: Step 3: Decide whether to fix, refactor or rebuild
div.p: There's no universal answer, and anyone who recommends a full rebuild before looking at the code should be treated with caution. The audit should support one of three choices:

ol.li: Fix. The foundation is sound. Finish the missing features and fix the bugs.
Refactor. The foundation is usable but parts need restructuring before you can build further.
Rebuild. The problems are deep enough that starting over is cheaper and safer over time.

div.p: Often it's a mix: keep what works, refactor what's fragile, rebuild the parts that matter most for growth.

blockquote.p: Sometimes fixing beats rewriting, and sometimes it doesn't. You should know which, with costs, before you commit.

div.p: Before adding anything new, fix what could hurt you:

ul.li: Critical bugs affecting users or operations.
Security gaps.
Deployment problems that make releases risky.

div.p: Stabilizing first gives your team a platform they can actually use while the rest of the work continues.
div.h2: Step 5: Finish in short, visible steps
div.p: Rebuild confidence by delivering working software every few weeks. Short sprints with demos let you see progress, steer priorities and catch misunderstandings early, which is often exactly what was missing with the previous vendor.

The Arc, a news platform covering India's high-growth companies, came to us after its previous vendor walked away in the middle of development. Editorial tools were incomplete, internal features were unfinished, and the reader-facing site needed to perform.

We didn't scrap everything and start from scratch. We started with a thorough audit and knowledge transfer, stabilized the platform, and patched critical security issues so the editorial desk could work properly. Then we finished and refined the existing features, moved the reader site to Next.js and built a custom CMS for the journalists.
The Arc now serves 50,000+ visitors a month, with PageSpeed scores ahead of its competitors.
div.h2: Sometimes you need people, not a takeover
div.p: Not every stalled project needs a new vendor to take over. Sometimes the internal team is capable but overloaded, or the codebase has accumulated technical debt that slows every new feature.

For Fashquik, a marketplace that helps local vendors sell to nearby customers, our developers joined their own team to optimize the codebase, re-engineer vendor management and rebuild delivery dispatch, getting the marketplace scaling again.
div.h2: How to avoid ending up here again
div.p: Once the project is back on track, put a few protections in place:

ul.li: Own your code and accounts. Make it contractual that the code and data belong to you once paid for.
Keep the code in your repository, not the vendor's.
Require documentation as part of every delivery.
Insist on regular demos of working software, not just status reports.
Agree on a handover process in the contract, before you need it.

div.p: A vendor walking away mid-build is painful, but it's rarely fatal. Secure your assets, get an honest audit, decide on fix, refactor or rebuild based on evidence, stabilize first and finish in visible steps. With the right partner, a stalled project can become a stronger platform than the one you originally planned.

Your Website Gets Traffic but No Enquiries. Here's What to Fix First.
For many B2B companies the website isn't short of visitors. It's short of a clear path from visitor to conversation.
For many B2B companies the website isn't short of visitors. It's short of a clear path from visitor to conversation.

div.p: Many companies assume their website problem is traffic. If only more people visited, more enquiries would follow.
Often, that isn't the problem. The visitors are already there. They arrive, look around and leave without getting in touch. Sending more people to the same site just means more people leaving.
The real issue is conversion: how well the website turns a visitor into a conversation.
div.h2: Signs your website has a conversion problem

ul.li: Reasonable traffic, but very few form submissions or calls.
High bounce rates on key pages.
Visitors on mobile leaving faster than those on desktop.
Sales hears "I couldn't tell what you do" or "I wasn't sure who to contact".
Enquiries arrive by email but never make it into the CRM.

div.p: Visitors can't quickly understand what you offer, who it's for or why it matters. If the homepage talks about your company more than the buyer's problem, many visitors won't stay long enough to find out.
The right page exists, but it's hard to find. Too many menu items, unclear labels or services buried several clicks deep.
Ten different buttons, or none at all. Visitors need one clear next step on every page.
Different buyers have different questions. A CFO, an operations head and a technical lead look for different things. A single generic page rarely speaks to all of them.
Many B2B buyers first visit on their phone. If the site is hard to use on mobile, that first impression is the last.
Enquiries land in a shared inbox, get forwarded, and sometimes get lost. If forms don't feed your CRM directly, follow-ups depend on someone remembering.
The most expensive mistake is redesigning based on opinions. Before changing anything, find out where visitors actually hesitate and leave:

ul.li: Heatmaps show where people click, scroll and stop.
Behavior recordings show how people move through the site.
Short visitor surveys reveal what people came for and what they couldn't find.
Analytics show which pages lose the most visitors.

div.p: Every change should target a real drop-off point.

blockquote.p: Traffic is rarely the first thing to fix. The path from visitor to enquiry usually is.

div.p: MaxintelB2B, a B2B data and lead generation company, had traffic but few leads. Navigation was confusing, calls to action were scattered and the mobile experience was poor. For a lead generation company, a website that doesn't generate leads is a credibility problem.

We started with surveys, heatmaps and behavior tracking. Then we rebuilt the navigation, created a landing page for each audience segment with one focused call to action, made the site fully responsive and connected lead capture directly to HubSpot.
The result: 15% more conversions across the site and 30% more high-intent B2B leads, with far fewer mobile drop-offs.

FYHBA Medical Billing, a US medical billing and coding company, had substantial traffic but low lead generation. The interface was complicated, services weren't clearly presented and the site didn't work well on phones.

We redesigned it around what medical practices need to know before getting in touch: simpler navigation, clear service pages, responsive design, lead forms at decision points and automated appointment scheduling.
The result: 32% more leads and a 35% lower bounce rate.
Review your site against these questions:

ol.li: Can a new visitor tell what you do, and for whom, within five seconds of landing?
Is there one clear next step on every important page?
Do your main buyer types each have a page that speaks to their concerns?
Does the site work as well on a phone as on a laptop?
Do you show proof: real results, client names and testimonials?
Does every form feed your CRM automatically?
Can visitors book a call without email back-and-forth?
Do you know which pages lose the most visitors?

div.p: Once changes are live, track:

ul.li: Conversion rate. Enquiries as a share of visitors, overall and by page.
Lead quality. How many enquiries match your ideal customer.
Bounce rate on key pages. Especially service and landing pages.
Time to follow up. How quickly sales responds once an enquiry arrives.

div.p: A website with traffic and no enquiries doesn't need more visitors. It needs a clearer path. Research where people drop off, make every page answer the buyer's question, give one clear next step and connect every form to your CRM. Those changes usually deliver more than any traffic campaign.

How to Choose a Technology Partner: 12 Questions to Ask Before You Sign
The right partner can save a growing company years of rework. The wrong one can cost just as much. These questions help you tell the difference.
The right partner can save a growing company years of rework. The wrong one can cost just as much. These questions help you tell the difference.

div.p: As a company grows, technology becomes a bigger part of the business than anyone planned. New processes appear, teams expand and systems multiply. At some point, leaders face a choice:

ul.li: Build everything with an internal team.
Manage several specialist vendors.
Find a technology partner who can grow alongside the business.

div.p: Building a full internal team for every need is slow and expensive. Juggling vendors with different priorities is often worse. That's why many growing companies look for a partner who sits in between: close enough to understand the business, flexible enough to change with it.
Choosing that partner is a high-stakes decision. Here are twelve questions to ask before you sign.
div.h3: 1. What do you want to know about our business before proposing anything?
div.p: A good partner asks about your bottlenecks, decisions and processes before talking about technology. If the first meeting is a product demo, be cautious.
div.h3: 2. Will you tell us if we don't need what we're asking for?
div.p: Sometimes the right answer is a small automation, not a big project, or no new software at all. A partner willing to say so is more likely to recommend what's right for you later.
div.h3: 3. How will we measure whether this worked?
div.p: Look for answers tied to business outcomes: hours saved, faster turnaround, more leads, fewer errors. Not just features delivered or tickets closed.
div.h3: 4. Can you show us similar work, with real results?
div.p: Ask for case studies with specific before-and-after numbers, and for client names or references where possible. Vague claims about "transforming businesses" tell you very little.
div.h3: 5. Who will actually work on our project?
div.p: The people in the sales meeting aren't always the people who build your system. Ask who will be on the team, what they've worked on and how much of their time you'll get.
div.h3: 6. Which pricing model do you recommend for us, and why?
div.p: The main options are:

ul.li: Fixed price, paid by milestone. Best for projects with a clear scope, such as a website, an ERP rollout or a new portal.
Time and material. Best when the scope will change as you learn, such as product development or project rescues. You should see the hours in timesheets.
Monthly retainer. Best for ongoing support, maintenance, hosting and small improvements, with response times agreed upfront.

div.p: A good partner explains which fits your situation, not just which suits them.
div.h3: 7. What exactly is included in the quote?
div.p: Ask what's not included: hosting, licenses, third-party services, data migration, training, support after launch. What you're quoted should be what you pay.
div.h3: 8. How do you handle changes in scope?
div.p: Scope always changes. Ask how changes are requested, estimated and approved, so there are no surprises on the invoice.
div.h3: 9. How often will we see working software?
div.p: Regular demos every few weeks let you steer while the work happens. Monthly status reports without working software are a warning sign.
div.h3: 10. Who owns the code and the data?
div.p: The answer should be clear and written into the contract: once the project is paid for, the code written for you and all your data belong to your company. Ask where the code will be stored, and make sure you have access to the repository.
div.h3: 11. Will you sign an NDA before seeing our code or data?
div.p: A professional partner should be comfortable signing a confidentiality agreement before reviewing anything sensitive.
Many problems appear only once real people use a system. Ask:

ul.li: How long does support last after launch?
Who answers questions six months later?
What are the response times for urgent issues?
What does ongoing maintenance cost?

div.p: The best answer is that the people who built your system are the people who support it.

blockquote.p: The best partnerships happen when the partner is treated as an extension of the team, and behaves like one.

ul.li: A proposal before they've understood your business.
No examples of similar work with measurable results.
Unclear ownership of code, data or accounts.
A large fixed price with a vague scope.
No plan for support after launch.
Pressure to sign quickly.

div.p: Many growing companies work with partners in other countries. That can work very well, provided you agree upfront on:

ul.li: Overlapping working hours for calls.
How progress is shared, such as project boards, demos and written updates.
Who your main point of contact is.
How urgent issues are handled outside normal hours.

div.p: The right technology partner understands your business before recommending technology, prices honestly, gives you full ownership of what you pay for and stays after launch. Ask these twelve questions of anyone you're considering, and the answers will tell you most of what you need to know.
